Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Vignette:
Javier had been a detective for four years, and he had always prided himself on his ability to read a room, to see past the surface of what people showed him. He could spot a liar from across an interrogation table. He had never imagined he could be so blind to what was happening in his own home. The relationship had started with a kind of intensity that he mistook for passion—his ex-partner, a man he had trusted completely, had a way of making Javier feel like the center of the universe, and then, slowly, like the cause of every problem. The first slap came during an argument about nothing, a Tuesday night, and Javier had been so stunned that he had convinced himself it was an accident. But the accidents kept happening. The last night, the night that ended everything, had started with the smell of whiskey on his partner’s breath. Javier had felt his stomach turn, a wave of nausea that he now recognized as a warning his body had understood before his mind did. His partner had grabbed him by the collar, and Javier had heard the fabric rip, a sound that now played in his head whenever a memory forced its way in. He had ended up on the kitchen floor, a gash on his forearm from a broken plate, and when he finally looked up, he saw his partner standing over him with an expression of cold disgust. Javier had left that night and never gone back, but he had brought the memory with him.

In the months that followed, Javier found that his own mind had become a hostile environment. The memories were not vague or distant; they were startlingly clear and detailed, as if his brain had recorded the entire event in high definition and was now playing it back without his permission. He would be standing in the grocery store, and the smell of a man’s cologne—something like whiskey and leather—would hit him, and suddenly he was back on that kitchen floor, hearing the rip of his shirt and the sound of his own breathing. The nausea would rise in his throat, immediate and physical, and he would have to abandon his cart and leave. At work, he was surrounded by violence. He saw injuries on victims and suspects every day—bruises, cuts, broken bones—and each one was a mirror held up to his own body. He found himself staring at a woman’s black eye during an interview, and he had to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he vomited. He had come to believe that he was marked by what had happened, that there was something fundamentally broken in him now that other people could sense. He was certain that he was permanently an outsider, that the easy camaraderie he used to have with his colleagues was gone. He had lost his faith in people entirely. They were not what they seemed, he thought. Everyone was capable of cruelty; he had just been too stupid to see it.

Javier’s response to this internal chaos was to build a fortress. He stopped letting anyone touch him. When his wife reached for his hand at dinner, he flinched, and he saw the hurt flicker across her face before she pulled away. He could not explain it to her—how a simple touch felt like a trap, like a prelude to a blow. He had learned to numb his feelings, to push everything down into a cold, flat place where it could not hurt him. Even relaxation felt dangerous. On the rare evenings he tried to sit on the couch and watch a movie, his heart would start racing within minutes, his body bracing for an attack that was not coming. So he stopped trying. He worked longer hours, took the night shifts no one else wanted, and filled every waking moment with the mechanical tasks of his job. The consequence was that his marriage began to feel like a ghost of itself. His wife slept on the far side of the bed, and they spoke mostly about logistics. He knew she was lonely, but he did not know how to let her back in.

What finally brought Javier to seek help was a moment at his desk. He had been reviewing case files, and a photograph of a victim’s facial injuries triggered a memory so vivid that he heard his own voice pleading, a sound he had not known he had made that night. He sat frozen, staring at nothing, for nearly ten minutes. When he came back to himself, he realized he was terrified—not of his ex-partner, but of his own mind. He was afraid that the fortress was going to collapse, and that he would be left with nothing but the memory and the nausea and the certainty that he would never feel safe again. He hoped, quietly and without much conviction, that someone could show him a way out.
